w: Ceaușescu ordered the world's heaviest building: 4,098,500 tonnes of marble and gilt, dug 92 metres into the hill, raised by 700 architects between 1984 and 1997. He was executed two years before it was finished. The Independent called it hideous but also sort of impressive. Understatement.
s: World's heaviest building. Built by a dictator.
_facts: Ordered by Nicolae Ceaușescu; built 1984-1997 with ~700 architects
Heaviest building in the world at about 4,098,500 tonnes; 84m tall, 92m deep
Largest civilian administrative building in the world
The Independent called it 'hideous but also sort of impressive'

w: Built to face down the Palace of Parliament across Arsenal Square, the People's Salvation Cathedral is the tallest and largest Orthodox church on earth: 133 metres high, the world's biggest free-swinging bell, and — once finished — 25,000 square metres of mosaic. Consecrated in 2018; still being gilded.
s: World's biggest Orthodox cathedral, still being gilded
_facts: 133 metres tall; tallest and largest Orthodox church by volume/area in the world
Faces the Palace of Parliament across Arsenal Square on Spirea's Hill
Will have the world's largest collection of church mosaics (~25,000 sq m) and largest iconostasis
Consecrated 25 November 2018; mosaic consecration followed in 2025

w: Romania's biggest stadium has held a Europa League final, four Euro 2020 matches, and gigs by Metallica and Guns N' Roses — but its strangest night was in 2021, when the retractable-roof bowl hosted Dota 2's world championship and set an esports prize-pool record that still stands.
s: 55,000-seat stadium that once hosted an esports final
_facts: 55,634 seats; largest stadium in Romania, opened 2011 with a retractable roof
Hosted the 2012 UEFA Europa League final and four UEFA Euro 2020 matches
Hosted The International 2021 Dota 2 championship, still holding the Guinness record for largest esports prize pool ($40,018,195)
Has hosted concerts by Metallica, Guns N' Roses, RHCP, Depeche Mode and Ed Sheeran; home of FCSB

w: A tiny Brâncovenesc-style church that was demoted to an ordinary parish when its monastery was dissolved, then reopened as a convent for nuns anyway. The name comes from the Greek for 'city of the Cross.' The real draw is inside: Romania's largest collection of Byzantine music manuscripts, still sung by the choir.
s: Tiny convent holding Romania's Byzantine-music archive
_facts: Eastern Orthodox monastery for nuns in central Bucharest, church built in Brâncovenesc style
Name is Greek for 'city of the Cross'; was known simply as Stavropoleos Church when the monastery was dissolved
Dedicated to the Archangels Michael and Gabriel
Holds the largest collection of Byzantine music books in Romania, tied to its choir
